what_its_for: Scopolamine is used to prevent nausea and vomiting caused by motion sickness (like car, boat, or plane travel) or after certain surgeries or medical procedures. It works by calming the part of your brain and inner ear that triggers nausea and vomiting.
how_to_take: Scopolamine most commonly comes as a small patch that you stick on your skin, usually behind your ear. Choose a dry, clean, hairless area of skin behind one ear. Press the patch firmly for about 30 seconds to make sure it sticks. Wash your hands thoroughly with soap and water right after applying or removing the patch — and avoid touching your eyes, as this can cause blurred vision or dilated pupils. Change to the other ear if you need a new patch. If it falls off, replace it behind the other ear. The patch should stay in place even while showering or swimming, but avoid direct water spray on it.
dosing: For motion sickness (patch): Apply ONE patch behind your ear at least 4 hours before you need it (some doctors recommend applying it the evening before travel). Each patch lasts up to 3 days (72 hours). Do not use more than one patch at a time. After removing the patch, fold it in half with the sticky side together and dispose of it safely, away from children and pets. For tablets (if prescribed): Follow your doctor's exact instructions, as the dose depends on your reason for taking it.
missed_dose: If you forget to apply the patch before your trip or activity and you are already feeling sick, apply it as soon as you remember — but it may take a few hours to work. Do not apply two patches at the same time to make up for a missed dose. If you are taking tablets and miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember. If it is almost time for your next dose, skip the missed one and continue your regular schedule. Never double up on doses.
storage: Store scopolamine patches and tablets at room temperature, between 68°F and 77°F (20°C to 25°C). Keep them in their original sealed pouches until you are ready to use them. Keep all medications out of reach of children and pets. Do not store in the bathroom or near heat, moisture, or direct sunlight.
what_to_avoid: Avoid drinking alcohol while using scopolamine — it can increase dizziness and drowsiness. Avoid driving, operating heavy machinery, or doing activities that require alertness until you know how this medication affects you, as it can cause significant drowsiness and blurred vision. Avoid touching your eyes after handling the patch — even tiny amounts of the medication can cause your pupil to become very large and affect your vision. Avoid using other medications that cause drowsiness (such as sleep aids, antihistamines, anxiety medications, or muscle relaxants) without talking to your doctor or pharmacist first. Avoid getting the patch wet directly (such as in a hot tub or under a direct shower stream).
when_to_call_doctor: Contact your doctor right away if you experience: severe confusion, agitation, or hallucinations (seeing or hearing things that are not there); difficulty urinating or no urination; severe eye pain or very blurred vision with redness of the eye (this could be a sign of a serious eye condition called acute angle-closure glaucoma); a fast or irregular heartbeat; severe skin redness, rash, or irritation where the patch is applied; high fever with flushing, dry mouth, and inability to sweat; or if you have a seizure. Also call your doctor if your nausea and vomiting do not improve or get worse.
when_it_works: The scopolamine patch usually starts working within 4 hours of being applied to your skin, which is why it should be applied well before you expect to be exposed to motion. The full effect is typically reached after about 8 hours. If you are using it for motion sickness, it works best when applied the night before travel. Tablets generally start working within 1 to 2 hours.
special_populations: Older adults (65+): Use with extra caution. Scopolamine can cause more pronounced confusion, memory problems, dizziness, and falls in older adults. It is listed as a potentially inappropriate medication for seniors. Talk to your doctor about whether it is the right choice for you. Children: The patch is generally not recommended for children. Tablets may be used in some older children under a doctor's guidance. Pregnancy: Talk to your doctor before using scopolamine if you are pregnant or planning to become pregnant. Breastfeeding: This medication may pass into breast milk. Consult your doctor before using it while breastfeeding. Kidney or liver problems: Let your doctor know if you have kidney or liver disease, as dose adjustments may be needed. Glaucoma: Do NOT use scopolamine if you have narrow-angle glaucoma or a personal or family history of glaucoma without speaking to your eye doctor first, as it can worsen this condition.
